name: TokuDB / PerconaFT Fractal Tree Index
baseline: MongoDB's default B-tree index (MMAPv1 storage engine)
workload: Multikey index insertion benchmark: 3.5M documents inserted into MongoDB v2.2.RC0, each document with a 100-entry array field (URI), forcing 100 index operations per insert
claimed_speedup: 532x insert throughput at 3.5M documents (2.11 inserts/sec on stock MongoDB vs 1,124.36 inserts/sec with TokuDB/Fractal Tree indexes)
hardware: Sun x4150, 2x Xeon 5460, 16GB RAM, StorageTek RAID controller (256MB write-back cache), 4x10K RPM SAS drives in RAID 0, Ubuntu 10.04 Server 64-bit, ext4
stars_or_usage: 562 stars; formerly shipped as TokuDB/TokuMX, now maintained by Percona as PerconaFT
tradeoffs: Write-optimized Fractal Tree (buffered B-tree family) index trades some point-lookup latency and extra CPU/memory for message buffering in exchange for much higher sustained insert throughput on write- and index-heavy workloads; requires the TokuDB/PerconaFT storage engine rather than being a drop-in library; different compression/crash-recovery model than a plain B-tree
caveats: First-party vendor blog post (Tokutek, later acquired into Percona); MongoDB v2.2.RC0 baseline is a very old pre-WiredTiger MMAP engine known to serialize writes behind a single global lock, so the 532x figure is inflated by that baseline's severe write bottleneck rather than purely algorithmic superiority; no compiler flags stated; original tokutek.com site is now a dead/parked domain, page recovered via web.archive.org
found_via: Blogs / talks: HN Algolia query 'fractal+tree+index' -> Tokutek company blog '532x Multikey Index Insertion Performance Increase for MongoDB with Fractal Tree Indexes'

name: MyRocks (RocksDB storage engine for MySQL)
baseline: InnoDB B-tree storage engine (MySQL / Percona Server 5.7)
workload: sysbench-tpcc, 100 warehouses / 10 tables (~90GB dataset under InnoDB, 21GB under MyRocks with LZ4), varying buffer pool / block cache size from 5GB to 100GB, binlog enabled, READ-COMMITTED isolation
claimed_speedup: ~5x higher tps at low memory budgets (4205.7 vs 849.1 tps at 5GB cache); the advantage shrinks and reverses as memory grows, with InnoDB ~30% faster than MyRocks at 100GB (5961.2 vs 4599.1 tps)
hardware: Supermicro server, Intel Xeon E5-2683 v3 @2.00GHz (2 sockets / 28 cores / 56 threads), 256GB RAM, Samsung SM863 1.9TB SSD, ext4, Ubuntu 16.04.4 (kernel 4.13.0-36), Percona Server 5.7.21-20
stars_or_usage: 2.6k stars; used in production at Facebook/Meta and shipped by Percona Server and MariaDB
tradeoffs: LSM-tree write-optimized engine achieves much better compression (21GB vs 90GB dataset here) and far higher tps under constrained memory, but unlike a B-tree it does not keep improving as more cache/RAM is added, so InnoDB overtakes it once the working set fits in the buffer pool; at benchmark time MyRocks lacked FOREIGN KEY support and SELECT..FOR UPDATE under REPEATABLE-READ in this Percona Server version
caveats: Independent (Percona) benchmark rather than Facebook's own, with published tuning scripts (Percona-Lab-results GitHub repo), hardware and software versions fully stated, but no compiler/build flags given (this is a server-level benchmark, not a microbenchmark); the win is workload/memory-dependent, not universal -- the author explicitly frames InnoDB as the baseline and shows InnoDB winning at high memory; repo is now archived on GitHub with an unclear/NOASSERTION license
found_via: Blogs / talks: HN Algolia query 'MyRocks' -> Percona Database Performance Blog 'A Look at MyRocks Performance' by Vadim Tkachenko

name: Wormhole (fast ordered index)
baseline: skip list (as used in LevelDB/RocksDB memtables), B+-tree, Adaptive Radix Tree (ART), Masstree
workload: Single- and multi-threaded (1-16 thread) point-lookup throughput over an in-memory ordered index built from real URL/webpage key data, on a dual-socket server
claimed_speedup: Up to 8.4x over skip list, 4.9x over B+-tree, 4.3x over ART, and 6.6x over Masstree in single-thread key-lookup throughput; 1.266 MOPS vs ART's 0.834 MOPS single-thread (52% higher); 19.5 MOPS vs ART at 16 threads (43% higher)
hardware: Dell R630, 2x 16-core Intel Xeon E5-2697A v4 (40MB LLC each), hyper-threading off, single NUMA node, 256GB DDR4-2400 ECC RAM, 64-bit Linux v4.15.15
tradeoffs: Combines a hash table, prefix trie, and B+-tree to keep fast range/point ops without sacrificing space versus B+-tree/skip list; concurrent access requires thread-local reference/RCU handles (wh_ref), adding a small per-op cost versus the thread-unsafe variant (~7.8% throughput loss when made thread-safe); plain C API, requires SSE4.2 on x86_64 or NEON+crc on AArch64
caveats: Evidence is the EuroSys'19 peer-reviewed paper/talk plus the authors' own reference implementation repo; hardware is fully specified but the paper does not state compiler or optimization flags used in the comparison (README says Clang is the default build compiler), which caps this at tier B rather than A; repo has had no commits since April 2022
found_via: Blogs / talks: HN Algolia query 'wormhole+index' -> EuroSys 2019 paper/talk 'Wormhole: A Fast Ordered Index for In-Memory Data Management' and its reference implementation repo
